newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK--U.S. heat seen hot, gasoline clearly not.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK--U.S. heat seen hot, gasoline clearly not.

text.p: The outlook in U.S. refined oil product markets is split between bullish views on heating oil and bearish views on gasoline, industry sources said.

Bullish sentiment around distillates centers on industry data showing heating oil stocks of 22 million barrels on the East Coast, the biggest heating oil market in the world, are a full 19 million barrels below year-ago levels.

But gasoline markets were burdened by views the arrival of numerous cargoes in the next few weeks will weigh heavily on a market characterized by flagging end-of-summer demand, and softening refinery profit margins.
"That's been the ongoing story for a while," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst at Cargill Investor Services in New York, referring to the split in U.S. product markets.

Industry sources said solid refining margins on heating oil will ease some pain for refiners faced with poor margins on gasoline. But analysts cautioned heating oil's strength is unlikely to completely offset gasoline's weakness.

"Distillates can't help overall refinery margins much because they're just 20 percent of the barrel," said Ken Miller of the Houston consulting firm of Purvin & Gertz, adding gasoline would continue to drag down refinery profits.
Indeed, nearby NYMEX gasoline futures for October delivery shed 0.23 on Friday settling at 61.09 cents a gallon.

In cash markets, the prompt spot New York Harbor regular reformulated unleaded gasoline has slipped 10 percent in the past week to 60.75 cents a gallon Friday, while regular conventional in Houston shed about five percent.

Predictably, heating oil prices on the NYMEX moved higher on Friday, with October heat settling 0.65 cent higher at 67.42 cents a gallon -- well below the week-ago intraday high of 70.15 cents but still at levels not usually reached until the dead of winter.

But spot markets have settled down since a group of distillate cargoes were fixed during recent weeks for shipment to Europe from the United States in volumes that have made concerns surrounding low distillate stocks much more acute.
"Seventy cents a gallon and above heating oil is clearly speculative," said Cargill's Blakeslee, noting those levels were unrealistically high ahead of winter.

"The heating oil market is going to be extremely sensitive to every five-day weather report," Blakeslee said, noting low heating oil inventories will make distillate markets far more volatile than they have been in the past.
